title: When Does Sparse Routing Help?The Geometry of Expert Separation in Mixture of Experts

paper.title: When Does Sparse Routing Help? The Geometry of Expert Separation in Mixture of Experts
paper.abstract: Abstract Sparse mixtures of experts combine multiple prediction models while evaluating only a small subset for each input. Although this architecture reduces computation, how expert separation and routing sparsity jointly govern expert recovery remains an open problem. In this paper, we address this question for location Gaussian mixtures of experts with a fixed number of experts by establishing how expert separation and spatial arrangement determine recovery rates. For dense models, our results reveal that when experts form well-separated clusters, the separation geometry is governed by the size of the largest cluster; without a prescribed cluster structure, this geometry is instead driven by the total number of experts. For sparse models, the separation geometry on retained routing regions is determined by the number of active experts, while the contribution of omitted regions is controlled by their total probability. Consequently, activating fewer experts reduces the separation complexity in these bounds. Furthermore, Top-1 routing yields a particularly striking result: experts can be recovered at a rate independent of the separation quantity. Our technical approach combines polynomial interpolation and Gaussian reproducing-kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) test functions with quantitative restriction inequalities that extend pointwise comparisons to expert functions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Mixtures of experts (MoE) model heterogeneous input–output relationships by combining several prediction rules through an input-dependent gate [ 19 , 21 ] . The prediction rules, called experts , may be regression functions, classifiers, or neural networks. The gate assigns weights to their outputs, allowing the contribution of each expert to vary across the input space. This structure accommodates differences between subpopulations while retaining a common predictive model. Sparse MoE limits the number of experts evaluated at each input. A Top- K K router selects the K K highest-scoring experts and combines their outputs using normalized weights. The architecture can therefore increase its total parameter count while controlling the computation per input [ 37 , 11 ] . Applications include multilingual machine translation [ 25 ] , language modeling [ 10 , 20 ] , image recognition [ 36 ] , and multimodal learning [ 14 ] . More recent architectures, including DeepSeekMoE, explicitly seek to encourage specialization and reduce redundancy among experts [ 8 ] .

sections.heading: From predictive accuracy to expert recovery.
sections.text: Specialization motivates a statistical problem distinct from prediction: estimating the individual expert functions from observations of the aggregate conditional law. Existing MoE theory studies the identifiability and estimation of this latent decomposition, including interactions between expert and gate parameters [ 18 , 34 ] . The accuracy of a fitted conditional density need not translate into comparable accuracy for its constituent experts. When experts give similar predictions where they are jointly active, changes in their functions and weights can partially cancel in the mixture. Related distinguishability results show that overlap between a fixed expert and a trainable expert can substantially slow parameter estimation [ 42 ] . We study this loss of information directly through functional recovery losses, which quantify the estimability of expert functions up to an appropriate matching of labels.

sections.heading: Why separation geometry matters.
sections.text: Separation determines how stably the conditional density identifies its latent experts. At a fixed covariate, nearby Gaussian means can produce similar component densities, allowing appreciable changes in the mixing distribution to have a small effect on the observable law. Quantitative mixture-identification bounds and cluster-adaptive estimation results make this dependence explicit [ 35 , 41 ] . A minimum distance alone does not describe the configuration: a collection of small, well-separated clusters presents different local inverse problems from a single cluster containing all experts. In MoE, these configurations also vary with the covariate. Functional separation must therefore be related to pointwise separation on sufficiently informative subsets of 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . Sparse routing adds the requirement that experts be distinguishable where they are active, with the probabilities of those regions determining their contribution to the recovery loss. Our bounds track these features through cluster size, the active count, and conditional geometry. This leads to two questions. Question: How do separation, sparsity, and cluster structure affect expert recovery?

sections.heading: Parameter and expert estimation in MoE.
sections.text: Much of the statistical theory of MoE concerns identifiability and parameter estimation. Ho et al. [ 18 ] study Gaussian MoE with covariate-free gates, and Nguyen et al. [ 34 ] analyze parameter interactions in softmax-gated Gaussian MoE. For hard Top- K K gates, Nguyen et al. [ 28 ] establish density and parameter rates using losses that account for the routing partition. Related results concern sigmoid gates [ 31 ] , the perturbed cosine router [ 29 ] , and Bayesian softmax MoE [ 1 ] . These works identify the expert family, gating mechanism, and specification of the expert count as determinants of estimation difficulty. Expert estimation is often studied by transferring parameter rates through regularity of the expert map. For instance, Nguyen et al. [ 30 ] use inequalities of the form ‖ h ⁡ ( ⋅ , η ^ ) − h ⁡ ( ⋅ , η ∗ ) ‖ L p ​ ( P X ) ≤ L ​ ‖ η ^ − η ∗ ‖ 2 . \|h(\cdot,\widehat{\eta})-h(\cdot,\eta^{*})\|_{L^{p}(P_{X})}\leq L\|\widehat{\eta}-\eta^{*}\|_{2}. This inequality transfers an upper bound, but does not show that the resulting rate is optimal for the functional target. Parameter perturbations can produce much smaller changes in the expert function. Moreover, constants that depend implicitly on the true model do not quantify deterioration as experts approach one another. We address these issues by proving inverse inequalities directly for functional losses and tracking their dependence on separation. The results concern different targets and assumptions from much of the parameter-based theory, and should be compared on that basis.

sections.heading: MoE theory in deep learning.
sections.text: Another line of work studies how routing and expert specialization affect learning in neural architectures. For a classification problem with clustered inputs, Chen et al. [ 6 ] show that a router can learn cluster-center features and divide the problem among two-layer convolutional experts, enabling learning where a single expert struggles. Chowdhury et al. [ 7 ] establish sample-complexity improvements from patch-level routing for mixtures of two-layer convolutional networks, showing how routing informative patches to experts can improve generalization. In continual learning, Li et al. [ 26 ] analyze sequential overparameterized linear regression tasks and characterize how expert specialization and routing affect expected forgetting and generalization error. Their analysis also shows that increasing the number of experts can delay convergence without necessarily improving performance. Connecting MoE to transformer adaptation, Le et al. [ 24 ] represent attention through linear experts with quadratic gating scores and interpret prefix tuning as adding task-specific experts, motivating a new gating mechanism for prompt-based continual learning. These studies provide theoretical explanations for specialization, sample efficiency, and adaptation under their respective model and data assumptions. Our results complement these perspectives by quantifying how separation between latent expert functions and the number of simultaneously active experts affect statistical recovery rates in Gaussian MoE.

sections.heading: Separation in finite mixture models.
sections.text: In finite-mixture models, quantitative identifiability inequalities connect density estimation to recovery of the mixing measure in Wasserstein distance [ 35 , 17 , 15 ] . For Gaussian location mixtures, Wu and Yang [ 41 ] obtain rates that adapt to separated clusters using moment comparison and polynomial interpolation. Nguyen et al. [ 33 ] further track separation and minimum-weight dependence in single-cluster, multiple-cluster, and unstructured configurations. Extending this perspective to MoE requires an additional step. The mixture atoms now vary with the covariate, and pointwise recovery need not yield a common matching of whole expert functions. Sparse routing also requires control of the probability and geometry of the regions on which particular experts are active.

sections.heading: 1.2 Contributions and main findings
sections.text: Our main contribution is to quantify how separation between expert functions affects their recovery from the aggregate conditional density. The likelihood density error has rate log ⁡ n / n \sqrt{\log n/n} for fixed architecture, without a separation assumption. Recovering the individual experts requires an additional inverse step, whose stability depends on their separation. We make this dependence explicit in upper bounds for the experts’ mean absolute errors, showing how the separation penalty changes with cluster structure and the number of simultaneously active experts. Throughout, the Gaussian variance is known and common, and the fitted and true expert counts agree. The rates below hold under the corresponding likelihood, geometry, and restriction hypotheses, with the remaining constants uniform as Δ sep \Delta_{\mathrm{sep}} varies. (i) Separation controls recovery of globally matched dense experts. For dense MoE without a prescribed cluster partition, we obtain the expert recovery bound 𝒪 P ​ ( Δ sep − ( 2 ​ k − 2 ) ​ log ⁡ n / n ) \mathcal{O}_{P}\!\left(\Delta_{\mathrm{sep}}^{-(2k-2)}\sqrt{\log n/n}\right) for the maximum mean absolute error of the matched expert functions over the full covariate domain. One global permutation matches all fitted and true experts. The bound makes explicit how the guarantee deteriorates as the minimum separation decreases, even though the density estimation rate remains unchanged. It requires neither fitted localization nor an error condition relative to separation (Theorem 3.11 and Corollary 5.3 (ii)). Cluster structure refines this dependence. When the true experts form separated clusters with largest size s max s_{\max} , the corresponding bound becomes 𝒪 P ​ ( Δ sep − ( 2 ​ s max − 2 ) ​ log ⁡ n / n ) \mathcal{O}_{P}\!\left(\Delta_{\mathrm{sep}}^{-(2s_{\max}-2)}\sqrt{\log n/n}\right) under one cluster-preserving matching (Theorem 3.6 and Corollary 5.3 (i)). Thus the largest cluster, rather than the total number of experts, governs the displayed penalty for shrinking within-cluster separation, with the between-cluster scale held fixed. Several-cluster recovery requires stable fitted cluster membership and the stated restriction conditions. These results distinguish configurations with the same minimum separation but different cluster sizes. (ii) Sparse routing reduces the separation exponent on active regions. For Top- K K routing with K ≥ 2 K\geq 2 , we obtain the retained-region expert recovery bound 𝒪 P ​ ( C K , λ − 1 ​ Δ sep − ( 2 ​ K − 2 ) ​ log ⁡ n / n ) , \mathcal{O}_{P}\!\left(C_{K,\lambda}^{-1}\Delta_{\mathrm{sep}}^{-(2K-2)}\sqrt{\log n/n}\right), where λ \lambda is a probability threshold and C K , λ C_{K,\lambda} depends on the conditional geometry and restriction constants. The error sums matched expert discrepancies over retained routing regions under the original covariate distribution. Under single-cluster geometry for the active true experts on those regions, the separation exponent is 2 ​ K − 2 2K-2 , compared with 2 ​ k − 2 2k-2 for the dense one-cluster bound (Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 5.6 ). This identifies a way sparse routing can moderate the effect of small separation: fewer Gaussian components need to be distinguished at each input. The regional guarantees also account for exposure. Extending the loss to all routing regions adds a remainder controlled by the square root of their omitted probability; Proposition 5.7 balances this remainder against deterioration of the conditional inverse constant. Matchings may differ across regions, and the target concerns expert values where they are active. Consequently, the smaller separation exponent alone does not establish better full-domain recovery of every latent expert. (iii) Top-1 permits recovery of the selected function without separation. With one active expert, the conditional law is a single Gaussian, and the selected expert function has mean absolute error 𝒪 P ​ ( log ⁡ n / n ) \mathcal{O}_{P}\!\left(\sqrt{\log n/n}\right) without expert-separation or quantitative restriction assumptions (Corollary 4.7 and Eq. ( 5.28 )). This guarantee remains valid when latent experts approach one another or coincide. It identifies the endpoint of the separation dependence: distinguishing simultaneously active components is unnecessary for the selected-function target. Recovering every latent expert under one global matching remains a different objective and requires additional exposure and matching conditions. The deterministic inverse inequalities establish these separation penalties directly for functional recovery losses; the likelihood results transfer them to statistical upper bounds. Verification for linear experts gives concrete settings in which the required assumptions hold. The bounds quantify the effect of separation on the recovery guarantees; matching lower bounds and optimality of the exponents remain open. sections.heading: Organization.
sections.text: Section 2 collects the notation and common assumptions. Section 3 develops dense recovery under clustered and unstructured geometries, and Section 4 treats Top- K K routing and the Top-1 specialization. Section 5 proves likelihood rates and transfers them to the recovery losses. Section 6 verifies the assumptions for linear experts, and Section 7 discusses the implications, limitations, and further directions. Appendices A – F contain the inverse and likelihood proofs and the linear verification; Appendix G explains the partial-transport structure of the proposed losses.

sections.text: The following assumptions concern the parameter spaces and expert family; each result specifies which it requires. Section 6 gives verification results for linear experts. Geometry and restriction conditions specific to each recovery target are introduced later. Assumption 2.1 (Compact parameter spaces, bounded experts, and covariate regularity) . (i) The logit parameter space Θ β ⊂ ℝ d x × ℝ \Theta_{\beta}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times\mathbb{R} and the expert parameter space Ω η ⊂ ℝ d η \Omega_{\eta}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{\eta}} are compact. Compactness and parameter continuity support finite covering arguments and existence of the dense MLE, while boundedness places all Gaussian means in a common interval [ 34 , 32 ] . Compact logits on the cube give B := sup x ∈ 𝒳 , β ∈ Θ β | β 1 ⊤ ​ x + β 0 | < ∞ B:=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X},\,\beta\in\Theta_{\beta}}|\beta_{1}^{\top}x+\beta_{0}|<\infty and the dense weight floor π i , G ( k ) ​ ( x ) , π j ∗ ​ ( x ) ≥ π ¯ k := e − 2 ​ B / k > 0 . \pi_{i,G}^{(k)}(x),\pi_{j}^{*}(x)\geq\underline{\pi}_{k}:=e^{-2B}/k>0. (2.7) Analyticity ensures that a nonzero expert difference has a null zero set, but does not by itself imply uniform restriction or anti-concentration. General ReLU networks fall outside this analytic framework. Assumption 2.2 (Positive functional separation) . The quantity Δ sep \Delta_{\mathrm{sep}} is strictly positive. The true expert functions are distinct, although they may agree at particular covariates. The inverse bounds track 0 < Δ sep ≤ 2 ​ M 0<\Delta_{\mathrm{sep}}\leq 2M explicitly and allow shrinking separation. Neither the likelihood density rates nor the Top-1 selected-function bound requires this assumption. Assumption 2.3 (Scale-adaptive generalized anti-concentration) . The density condition is stronger than this near-zero estimate and is not automatic for analytic experts: X 2 X^{2} for X ∼ Unif ⁡ ( [ − 1 , 1 ] ) X\sim\operatorname{Unif}([-1,1]) has an unbounded density near zero, and a nonzero constant difference has no density. Proposition 6.2 verifies the condition for homogeneous linear experts. Assumption 2.4 (Differentiability in the expert parameter) . The maps η ↦ h ⁡ ( ⋅ , η ) ∈ L 1 ​ ( P X ) and η ↦ h ⁡ ( ⋅ , η ) ∈ L ∞ ​ ( 𝒳 ) \eta\mapsto h(\cdot,\eta)\in L^{1}(P_{X})\quad\text{and}\quad\eta\mapsto h(\cdot,\eta)\in L^{\infty}(\mathcal{X}) are continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of Ω η \Omega_{\eta} . sections.heading: 3 Inverse Bounds for Dense MoE
sections.text: In this section, we establish inverse bounds connecting density recovery to expert recovery in dense MoE through the expert separation quantity Δ sep \Delta_{\mathrm{sep}} . We consider two main regimes: (i) the multi-cluster regime, in which the true experts are partitioned into separated clusters, with the single-cluster case included as a specialization; and (ii) the unstructured regime, in which no cluster partition or cluster geometry is prescribed. The latter retains the separation, anti-concentration, and restriction assumptions stated below.

sections.heading: 4 Inverse Bounds for Sparse MoE
sections.text: This section establishes deterministic inverse inequalities for active expert recovery under Top- K K routing. We first partition the covariate domain into regions on which the true and fitted active sets are fixed, and define a loss that matches experts within each region. For K ≥ 2 K\geq 2 , conditional separation and restriction assumptions yield an inverse bound with separation exponent 2 ​ K − 2 2K-2 on regions of probability at least τ \tau ; the remaining regions contribute a remainder controlled by their total probability. We then treat Top-1, for which the selected expert function admits a separation-free bound. Statistical rates follow by combining these inequalities with the likelihood results in Section 5 .

sections.heading: 5 From Inverse Bounds to Statistical Rates for MLE
sections.text: We now combine likelihood density estimation with the inverse inequalities of Sections 3 and 4 to obtain statistical recovery rates. Section 5.1 treats dense softmax models, and Section 5.2 treats hard Top- K K routing. In each case, we first bound the density error and then identify the additional geometric conditions needed to control the corresponding recovery loss. Throughout this section, assume the iid, correctly specified sampling model of Section 1 and Assumptions 2.1 and 2.4 . Use the MLEs defined there and write p ^ n := p G ^ n \widehat{p}_{n}:=p_{\widehat{G}_{n}} and p ^ n ( K ) := p G ^ n ( K ) ( K ) \widehat{p}_{n}^{(K)}:=p_{\widehat{G}_{n}^{(K)}}^{(K)} for their fitted densities. The density rates require no separation assumptions; recovery requires the relevant inverse hypotheses uniformly over the fitted class. Unless stated otherwise, the architecture is fixed.

sections.heading: 5.1 Density estimation and expert recovery in dense MoE
sections.text: We first derive covering bounds for the expert and logit classes and use them to establish a finite-sample density rate for the dense MLE. We then apply the inverse inequalities to obtain recovery rates for globally matched expert functions under clustered and unstructured geometries. Both transfers are direct deterministic comparisons; neither requires an additional localization event for the estimator.

sections.heading: 6 Assumptions Verification for Linear Experts
sections.text: This section gives concrete sufficient conditions for applying the recovery results to homogeneous linear experts. We first relate coefficient distances to functional separation and verify anti-concentration under the cube design. We then establish restriction for expert errors and give an elementary proof for binary softmax gates; Lemma C.4 covers general active counts. Coefficient clustering supplies dense and sparse geometry and an explicit threshold dependence for the sparse inverse constant. Fitted cluster compatibility remains a separate requirement for several-cluster recovery. Unstructured labelled recovery follows using the direct expert-restriction formulation of Theorem 3.11 .

sections.heading: 7 Discussion
sections.text: The goal of this paper is to understand when an accurate mixture-of-experts model also provides accurate estimates of its individual expert functions. This question matters whenever the experts themselves, and the distinctions between them, are part of the scientific or modeling objective. We study how expert separation and routing sparsity affect recovery from the aggregate conditional distribution. Our analysis concerns Gaussian experts with a known common variance and a correctly specified number of components, and measures recovery directly through errors in the expert functions. The main contributions describe how the arrangement and activation of experts influence their estimation. For dense models, we show that separated clusters can improve the dependence of the recovery bound on expert separation: the largest cluster governs the displayed separation penalty. We also obtain recovery under one global matching without a prescribed cluster partition. For sparse models, the number of simultaneously active experts determines the separation exponent on sufficiently informative routing regions, while the total probability of omitted regions controls their contribution to the error. Combining these bounds with likelihood density rates gives expert convergence guarantees under the corresponding geometric and restriction assumptions. Verification for linear experts provides concrete settings in which the results apply. These findings help explain why predictive accuracy alone may give an incomplete account of expert learning. Experts that produce similar outputs can be difficult to distinguish even when their combined distribution is estimated accurately. By making the dependence on separation explicit, the results quantify this source of instability and show how cluster structure can affect it. They also reveal a tradeoff in sparse routing: activating fewer experts reduces the difficulty of distinguishing components at a given input, but changes the information available about each expert across the input domain. Thus the choice of active count should reflect both the recovery objective and where the router exposes the experts to data. Top-1 gives a particularly clear implication. With one active expert, the conditional response law is a single Gaussian, so density accuracy directly controls the function selected at each input. Under the stated likelihood conditions, this selected function achieves the baseline convergence rate without a penalty for expert separation, even when latent experts approach one another or coincide. This provides a statistical reason to consider Top-1 when recovery of the selected function is the objective. The guarantee concerns that selected function; recovering every expert over its entire domain would additionally require sufficient exposure and a consistent correspondence between fitted and true experts across routing regions. The result therefore informs the choice of routing rule without establishing Top-1 as universally optimal for all expert-recovery tasks. Several directions follow from this distinction. One is to develop conditions that turn recovery on active regions into recovery of all expert functions under a common matching. Such conditions could clarify how routing coverage and overlap between active sets affect the information available about individual experts. Another is to develop data-driven methods for choosing the probability threshold used in the sparse recovery analysis, and eventually for selecting the active count itself. The present threshold calculation depends on separation and conditional geometry that may be unknown. Empirical studies could examine how well these theoretical quantities explain expert recovery in fitted models and whether they can guide practical routing choices. Further work should investigate the sharpness and computational scope of the guarantees. Matching lower bounds would determine whether the separation penalties and full-partition rates can be improved. Extending the analysis from global likelihood maximizers to approximate solutions would connect recovery accuracy to the behavior of practical training procedures. Broader model classes also merit study, including an unknown or over-specified number of experts, unequal or unknown variances, and more flexible expert and routing networks. These extensions would test how far the connection between separation, exposure, and functional recovery persists beyond the setting considered here. Appendices for “When Does Sparse Routing Help? The Geometry of Expert Separation in Mixture of Experts” Contents

sections.heading: Appendix A Separation Complexity of Gaussian Mixtures
sections.text: At each fixed covariate, recovery in the MoE model reduces to inversion of a univariate Gaussian location mixture. This appendix proves the scalar inverse inequalities used in the functional arguments, with explicit dependence on the separation of the true means. We combine Gaussian RKHS identities [ 2 , 38 ] , Wasserstein duality [ 40 ] , and Newton interpolation [ 9 ] . The proof constructs an RKHS function whose integral against the difference of the mixing measures controls their Wasserstein distance. Interpolation bounds the norm of this function in terms of true-support spacing. Lipschitz continuity controls the first divided difference without a separation factor; the higher orders determine the inverse exponent. For several support clusters, only divided differences within a cluster incur powers of the shrinking separation. Supremum and derivative bounds for interpolation are taken on [ − M , M ] [-M,M] unless another domain is specified. sections.heading: A.4 Gaussian inversion with separated support clusters
sections.text: The scalar bound can be sharpened when the union support occupies separated blocks. Divided differences within a block depend on its local spacing, whereas those spanning blocks have denominators bounded below by the macroscopic gap. This distinction yields an exponent determined by the largest block rather than the total number of components, in accordance with the localization used in finite-mixture separation bounds [ 33 ] . We first establish the interpolation estimate for consecutive support blocks and then apply it to Gaussian mixtures. The statement includes one block, for which the gap conditions disappear and Lemma A.5 applies directly. With several blocks, the fitted and true labels must have the stated allocation to separated full-support intervals.

sections.heading: Appendix B From Wasserstein Distance to Component Matching
sections.text: The scalar inverse inequalities control Wasserstein distance between conditional mixing measures. Functional recovery requires an additional comparison with a labelled matching cost that records expert displacement and gate error. This appendix establishes that comparison for one true cluster and for several separated clusters. The argument complements quantitative mixture-identification bounds in Wasserstein distance [ 35 , 17 , 16 ] . When matched weights differ, a permutation alone does not define a transport coupling. We therefore begin with an optimal labelled coupling [ 40 ] . Small transport cost forces a local matching and controls its weight discrepancies through off-diagonal mass. At larger cost, the cluster diameter bounds the displacement of any admissible pairing.

sections.heading: Appendix C Proofs for Results in Section 3
sections.text: This appendix transfers the scalar estimates to the dense labelled functional targets. We first construct a set of positive covariate probability on which the true expert values satisfy the required separation bounds. Under clustered geometry, scalar transport comparisons, a finite-permutation argument, and quantitative restriction yield one global matching. For unstructured recovery, a direct scalar density-to-matching bound replaces the diameter-dependent transport comparison. Class-wide transport restriction and an exponential Remez inequality supply the expert and gate restriction needed for the global loss.

sections.heading: Appendix D Proofs for Results in Section 4
sections.text: On each joint routing region, the true and fitted active sets are fixed and contain K K labels. The scalar inversion and matching estimates therefore apply to these active components under the conditional covariate law. This appendix proves Theorem 4.5 by aggregating regional inverse bounds and controlling omitted regions by their total probability. It then proves Corollary 4.7 and gives a sufficient condition for regional separation.

sections.heading: Appendix E Proofs for Results in Section 5
sections.text: This appendix proves the likelihood density rates and transfers them to the recovery losses. The dense argument uses a finite cover by pointwise upper functions. The sparse argument retains routing exactly, counts its realizable patterns on the sample, and covers the smooth expert and weight functions. Both arguments use likelihood affinity and finite-class probability bounds [ 39 , 3 ] , avoiding regular likelihood expansions that may fail at mixture singularities [ 13 ] . The density bounds require compact parameter spaces, uniformly bounded expert values, covariate continuity, and the L ∞ L^{\infty} parameter regularity in Assumption 2.4 . Analyticity enters only through covariate continuity. Separation, anti-concentration, and the inverse restriction assumptions are used only in the subsequent transfer to recovery. Estimators are assumed measurable; uniform empirical-process events are interpreted in outer probability when necessary.

sections.heading: Appendix G Partial Transport Interpretation of the Dense Recovery Losses
sections.text: This appendix explains the displacement and mass-discrepancy terms in the dense recovery losses through partial transport, which has also been used to characterize heterogeneous parameter estimation rates in finite mixture models [ 22 ] . We first distinguish prescribed transported mass from a penalty for unmatched mass. We then constrain transport to a fixed expert matching and compare maximal common-mass displacement with true-weighted displacement. The dense weight floor makes their functional versions equivalent. The transport penalty λ \lambda used here is distinct from the routing-probability threshold in Section 5.2 .

In labelled matrix form, Eq. ( G.3 ) becomes 𝖯𝖳 λ ​ ( x ) \displaystyle\mathsf{PT}_{\lambda}(x) : = 𝖯𝖳 λ ​ ( M G ∗ ​ ( x ) , M G ​ ( x ) ) \displaystyle:=\mathsf{PT}_{\lambda}(M_{G_{*}}(x),M_{G}(x)) (G.5) = min γ i ​ j ≥ 0 ∑ i γ i ​ j ≤ b j , ∑ j γ i ​ j ≤ a i ⁡ { ∑ i , j γ i ​ j ​ | s i − t j | + λ ⁡ ( 2 − 2 ​ ∑ i , j γ i ​ j ) } . \displaystyle=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\gamma_{ij}\geq 0\\ \sum_{i}\gamma_{ij}\leq b_{j},\ \sum_{j}\gamma_{ij}\leq a_{i}\end{subarray}}\left\{\sum_{i,j}\gamma_{ij}|s_{i}-t_{j}|+\lambda\left(2-2\sum_{i,j}\gamma_{ij}\right)\right\}. The entry γ i ​ j \gamma_{ij} transports mass from true label j j to fitted label i i . Retaining labels leaves the unrestricted optimum unchanged: mass at a shared numerical location can be distributed among its labels without changing the cost. Unrestricted conditional transport permits mass splitting and correspondences that vary with the covariate, as in the target D OT D_{\mathrm{OT}} . To compare individual experts, we instead fix an admissible permutation σ \sigma and restrict transport to the pairs j ↦ σ ⁡ ( j ) j\mapsto\sigma(j) . Section 3.1 uses the same permutation throughout the covariate domain; here we examine its cost at a fixed x x . (G.6) This is prescribed-mass partial transport subject to the fixed matching. Its largest feasible amount is α σ \alpha_{\sigma} . At that amount, all pairwise capacities are attained, so u j = m j u_{j}=m_{j} for every j j and 𝖯𝖮𝖳 α σ , σ ​ ( x ) = ∑ j m j ​ r j , 2 ​ ( 1 − α σ ) = ∑ j | a σ ⁡ ( j ) − b j | . \mathsf{POT}_{\alpha_{\sigma},\sigma}(x)=\sum_{j}m_{j}r_{j},\qquad 2(1-\alpha_{\sigma})=\sum_{j}|a_{\sigma(j)}-b_{j}|. (G.7) The second identity follows from 2 ​ min ⁡ { a , b } = a + b − | a − b | 2\min\{a,b\}=a+b-|a-b| and the fact that both weight vectors sum to one. Adding the unmatched-mass penalty to this prescribed-mass optimum gives 𝒫 λ , σ ​ ( x ) \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\lambda,\sigma}(x) : = 𝖯𝖮𝖳 α σ , σ ​ ( x ) + 2 ​ λ ​ ( 1 − α σ ) \displaystyle:=\mathsf{POT}_{\alpha_{\sigma},\sigma}(x)+2\lambda(1-\alpha_{\sigma}) (G.8) = ∑ j m j ​ r j + λ ​ ∑ j | a σ ⁡ ( j ) − b j | . \displaystyle=\sum_{j}m_{j}r_{j}+\lambda\sum_{j}|a_{\sigma(j)}-b_{j}|. The cost transports the largest common mass permitted by the matching and penalizes the residual mass on each side. For comparison, allowing the amount to vary under the same matching gives the penalized optimum 𝖯𝖳 λ , σ ​ ( x ) \displaystyle\mathsf{PT}_{\lambda,\sigma}(x) = min 0 ≤ α ≤ α σ ⁡ { 𝖯𝖮𝖳 α , σ ​ ( x ) + 2 ​ λ ​ ( 1 − α ) } \displaystyle=\min_{0\leq\alpha\leq\alpha_{\sigma}}\{\mathsf{POT}_{\alpha,\sigma}(x)+2\lambda(1-\alpha)\} (G.9) = min ⁡ ∑ j 0 ≤ u j ≤ m j ⁡ [ u j ​ r j + λ ⁡ { a σ ⁡ ( j ) + b j − 2 ​ u j } ] . \displaystyle=\min_{0\leq u_{j}\leq m_{j}}\sum_{j}\left[u_{j}r_{j}+\lambda\{a_{\sigma(j)}+b_{j}-2u_{j}\}\right]. Minimizing each linear summand yields 𝖯𝖳 λ , σ ​ ( x ) = ∑ j m j ​ min ⁡ { r j , 2 ​ λ } + λ ​ ∑ j | a σ ⁡ ( j ) − b j | . \mathsf{PT}_{\lambda,\sigma}(x)=\sum_{j}m_{j}\min\{r_{j},2\lambda\}+\lambda\sum_{j}|a_{\sigma(j)}-b_{j}|. (G.10) Indeed, u j = m j u_{j}=m_{j} is optimal when r j < 2 ​ λ r_{j}<2\lambda , u j = 0 u_{j}=0 is optimal when r j > 2 ​ λ r_{j}>2\lambda , and any amount is optimal at equality. sections.text: For an admissible permutation σ ∈ Σ 𝒞 \sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathcal{C}} , the three contributions to the loss are E σ \displaystyle E_{\sigma} : = ∑ j = 1 k ‖ π j ∗ ​ ( h σ ⁡ ( j ) − h j ∗ ) ‖ L 2 ​ ( P X ) , \displaystyle:=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\|\pi_{j}^{*}(h_{\sigma(j)}-h_{j}^{*})\|_{L^{2}(P_{X})}, expert displacement , \displaystyle\text{expert displacement}, (G.13) V σ \displaystyle V_{\sigma} : = Δ sep ​ ∑ j = 1 k ‖ π σ ⁡ ( j ) − π j ∗ ‖ L 1 ​ ( P X ) , \displaystyle:=\Delta_{\mathrm{sep}}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\|\pi_{\sigma(j)}-\pi_{j}^{*}\|_{L^{1}(P_{X})}, component mass discrepancy , \displaystyle\text{component mass discrepancy}, V 𝒞 \displaystyle V_{\mathcal{C}} : = ω q ​ ∑ m = 1 q ‖ Π m ​ ( ⋅ , G ) − Π m ∗ ‖ L 1 ​ ( P X ) , \displaystyle:=\omega_{q}\sum_{m=1}^{q}\|\Pi_{m}(\cdot;G)-\Pi_{m}^{*}\|_{L^{1}(P_{X})}, cluster mass discrepancy . \displaystyle\text{cluster mass discrepancy}. Thus D cluster = min σ ∈ Σ 𝒞 ⁡ ( E σ + V σ + V 𝒞 ) D_{\mathrm{cluster}}=\min_{\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathcal{C}}}(E_{\sigma}+V_{\sigma}+V_{\mathcal{C}}) . For several clusters, ω q = D 0 \omega_{q}=D_{0} and the permutation preserves the prescribed true and fitted blocks. The aggregate term V 𝒞 V_{\mathcal{C}} distinguishes redistribution within a block from net transfer between blocks. The former leaves the block mass unchanged, whereas the latter crosses a gap of order D 0 D_{0} on the informative set. This term is independent of the within-block permutation and retains control of mass discrepancies as the within-block separation decreases. Lemma B.2 bounds the component and cluster terms together by a single Wasserstein cost; they are not a decomposition of the cost of an optimal plan. The expert terms use L 2 ​ ( P X ) L^{2}(P_{X}) to match the covariate norm in the density error, while the mass terms use L 1 ​ ( P X ) L^{1}(P_{X}) to measure average absolute gate errors. Summing the component norms retains separate control of each matched expert and gate. These norms also specify the discrepancies to which the restriction assumptions apply. For each admissible σ \sigma , let m σ , j ​ ( x ) := min ⁡ { π σ ⁡ ( j ) ​ ( x ) , π j ∗ ​ ( x ) } . m_{\sigma,j}(x):=\min\{\pi_{\sigma(j)}(x),\pi_{j}^{*}(x)\}. The functional version of the common-mass cost, with the same norms and cluster correction as Definition 3.5 , is D partial , cluster ( G , G ∗ ) := min σ ∈ Σ 𝒞 { \displaystyle D_{\rm partial,cluster}(G,G_{*}):=\min_{\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathcal{C}}}\Bigg\{ ∑ j [ ‖ m σ , j ​ ( h σ ⁡ ( j ) − h j ∗ ) ‖ L 2 ​ ( P X ) + Δ sep ​ ‖ π σ ⁡ ( j ) − π j ∗ ‖ L 1 ​ ( P X ) ] \displaystyle\sum_{j}\Bigl[\|m_{\sigma,j}(h_{\sigma(j)}-h_{j}^{*})\|_{L^{2}(P_{X})}+\Delta_{\mathrm{sep}}\|\pi_{\sigma(j)}-\pi_{j}^{*}\|_{L^{1}(P_{X})}\Bigr] (G.14) + ω q ∑ m ∥ Π m ( ⋅ ; G ) − Π m ∗ ∥ L 1 ​ ( P X ) } . \displaystyle+\omega_{q}\sum_{m}\|\Pi_{m}(\cdot;G)-\Pi_{m}^{*}\|_{L^{1}(P_{X})}\Bigg\}. Denote its one-cluster specialization by D partial D_{\rm partial} . Proposition G.4 (Equivalence of the functional losses) . Under Eq. ( 2.7 ), D partial , cluster \displaystyle D_{\rm partial,cluster} ≤ D cluster ≤ π ¯ k − 1 ​ D partial , cluster , \displaystyle\leq D_{\mathrm{cluster}}\leq\underline{\pi}_{k}^{-1}D_{\rm partial,cluster}, (G.15) D partial \displaystyle D_{\rm partial} ≤ D func ≤ π ¯ k − 1 ​ D partial . \displaystyle\leq D_{\mathrm{func}}\leq\underline{\pi}_{k}^{-1}D_{\rm partial}. The constants are independent of Δ sep \Delta_{\mathrm{sep}} when k k and B B are fixed, and no localization of the fitted experts is needed for these comparisons. Proof. For every x , j , σ x,j,\sigma , π ¯ k ​ π j ∗ ​ ( x ) ≤ m σ , j ​ ( x ) ≤ π j ∗ ​ ( x ) \underline{\pi}_{k}\pi_{j}^{*}(x)\leq m_{\sigma,j}(x)\leq\pi_{j}^{*}(x) . Multiplication by the absolute expert difference and monotonicity of the L 2 L^{2} norm compare the displacement terms. The component and cluster mass terms are identical and nonnegative. Sum for each fixed permutation and then minimize over the same set of permutations. Taking q = 1 q=1 gives the second assertion. ∎ The equivalence compares two functional losses under the same admissible matching and cluster-mass correction. Taking component norms before minimizing preserves one correspondence between whole expert functions. Integrating unrestricted pointwise transport would allow the matching and mass allocation to vary with the covariate and would define a different recovery target. This structure also determines the clustered inverse argument in Appendix C.1 . Scalar inversion and the transport-to-matching comparison first control pointwise errors on an informative set. Selecting one permutation on a subset of positive probability then permits Assumptions 3.3 and 3.4 to extend its component and cluster-mass errors to the full domain, yielding precisely the norms in Eq. ( G.13 ).

The Geometry of Expert Separation in Mixture of Experts Huy Nguyen Dung Le Alessandro Rinaldo Nhat Ho Department of Statistics and Data Science The University of Texas at Austin November 1, 2026 Abstract Sparse mixtures of experts combine multiple prediction models while evaluating only a small subset for each input. Although this architecture reduces computation, how expert separation and routing sparsity jointly govern expert recovery remains an open problem. In this paper, we address this question for location Gaussian mixtures of experts with a fixed number of experts by establishing how expert separation and spatial arrangement determine recovery rates. For dense models, our results reveal that when experts form well-separated clusters, the separation geometry is governed by the size of the largest cluster; without a prescribed cluster structure, this geometry is instead driven by the total number of experts. For sparse models, the separation geometry on retained routing regions is determined by the number of active experts, while the contribution of omitted regions is controlled by their total probability. Consequently, activating fewer experts reduces the separation complexity in these bounds. Furthermore, Top-1 routing yields a particularly striking result: experts can be recovered at a rate independent of the separation quantity. Our technical approach combines polynomial interpolation and Gaussian reproducing-kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) test functions with quantitative restriction inequalities that extend pointwise comparisons to expert functions. 1 Introduction Mixtures of experts (MoE) model heterogeneous input–output relationships by combining several prediction rules through an input-dependent gate [ 19 , 21 ] . The prediction rules, called experts , may be regression functions, classifiers, or neural networks. The gate assigns weights to their outputs, allowing the contribution of each expert to vary across the input space. This structure accommodates differences between subpopulations while retaining a common predictive model. Sparse MoE limits the number of experts evaluated at each input. A Top- K K router selects the K K highest-scoring experts and combines their outputs using normalized weights. The architecture can therefore increase its total parameter count while controlling the computation per input [ 37 , 11 ] . Applications include multilingual machine translation [ 25 ] , language modeling [ 10 , 20 ] , image recognition [ 36 ] , and multimodal learning [ 14 ] . More recent architectures, including DeepSeekMoE, explicitly seek to encourage specialization and reduce redundancy among experts [ 8 ] . From predictive accuracy to expert recovery. Specialization motivates a statistical problem distinct from prediction: estimating the individual expert functions from observations of the aggregate conditional law. Existing MoE theory studies the identifiability and estimation of this latent decomposition, including interactions between expert and gate parameters [ 18 , 34 ] . The accuracy of a fitted conditional density need not translate into comparable accuracy for its constituent experts. When experts give similar predictions where they are jointly active, changes in their functions and weights can partially cancel in the mixture. Related distinguishability results show that overlap between a fixed expert and a trainable expert can substantially slow parameter estimation [ 42 ] . We study this loss of information directly through functional recovery losses, which quantify the estimability of expert functions up to an appropriate matching of labels. Problem setup. Dense clustered recovery provides one matching of whole expert functions and hence rates in this full-domain norm. The unstructured result also yields one global matching, without a cluster diameter or fitted-localization condition; class-wide transport restriction supplies the required expert restriction. Sparse recovery provides errors restricted to joint routing regions, where the corresponding experts are active, with matchings that may vary between regions. Full-domain recovery of each sparse expert requires additional exposure and matching conditions. The combined expert-and-gate losses introduced below are tools for deriving these conclusions, and also quantify gate-probability errors. Section 5 gives the likelihood rates and their transfer; the deterministic inverse inequalities apply to arbitrary admissible model pairs. Why separation geometry matters. Separation determines how stably the conditional density identifies its latent experts. At a fixed covariate, nearby Gaussian means can produce similar component densities, allowing appreciable changes in the mixing distribution to have a small effect on the observable law. Quantitative mixture-identification bounds and cluster-adaptive estimation results make this dependence explicit [ 35 , 41 ] . A minimum distance alone does not describe the configuration: a collection of small, well-separated clusters presents different local inverse problems from a single cluster containing all experts. In MoE, these configurations also vary with the covariate. Functional separation must therefore be related to pointwise separation on sufficiently informative subsets of 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . Sparse routing adds the requirement that experts be distinguishable where they are active, with the probabilities of those regions determining their contribution to the recovery loss. Our bounds track these features through cluster size, the active count, and conditional geometry. This leads to two questions. Question: How do separation, sparsity, and cluster structure affect expert recovery? 1.1 Related literature Parameter and expert estimation in MoE. Much of the statistical theory of MoE concerns identifiability and parameter estimation. Ho et al. [ 18 ] study Gaussian MoE with covariate-free gates, and Nguyen et al. [ 34 ] analyze parameter interactions in softmax-gated Gaussian MoE. For hard Top- K K gates, Nguyen et al. [ 28 ] establish density and parameter rates using losses that account for the routing partition. Related results concern sigmoid gates [ 31 ] , the perturbed cosine router [ 29 ] , and Bayesian softmax MoE [ 1 ] . These works identify the expert family, gating mechanism, and specification of the expert count as determinants of estimation difficulty. Expert estimation is often studied by transferring parameter rates through regularity of the expert map. For instance, Nguyen et al. [ 30 ] use inequalities of the form ‖ h ⁡ ( ⋅ , η ^ ) − h ⁡ ( ⋅ , η ∗ ) ‖ L p ​ ( P X ) ≤ L ​ ‖ η ^ − η ∗ ‖ 2 . \|h(\cdot,\widehat{\eta})-h(\cdot,\eta^{*})\|_{L^{p}(P_{X})}\leq L\|\widehat{\eta}-\eta^{*}\|_{2}. This inequality transfers an upper bound, but does not show that the resulting rate is optimal for the functional target. Parameter perturbations can produce much smaller changes in the expert function. Moreover, constants that depend implicitly on the true model do not quantify deterioration as experts approach one another. We address these issues by proving inverse inequalities directly for functional losses and tracking their dependence on separation. The results concern different targets and assumptions from much of the parameter-based theory, and should be compared on that basis. MoE theory in deep learning. Another line of work studies how routing and expert specialization affect learning in neural architectures. For a classification problem with clustered inputs, Chen et al. [ 6 ] show that a router can learn cluster-center features and divide the problem among two-layer convolutional experts, enabling learning where a single expert struggles. Chowdhury et al. [ 7 ] establish sample-complexity improvements from patch-level routing for mixtures of two-layer convolutional networks, showing how routing informative patches to experts can improve generalization. In continual learning, Li et al. [ 26 ] analyze sequential overparameterized linear regression tasks and characterize how expert specialization and routing affect expected forgetting and generalization error. Their analysis also shows that increasing the number of experts can delay convergence without necessarily improving performance. Connecting MoE to transformer adaptation, Le et al. [ 24 ] represent attention through linear experts with quadratic gating scores and interpret prefix tuning as adding task-specific experts, motivating a new gating mechanism for prompt-based continual learning. These studies provide theoretical explanations for specialization, sample efficiency, and adaptation under their respective model and data assumptions. Our results complement these perspectives by quantifying how separation between latent expert functions and the number of simultaneously active experts affect statistical recovery rates in Gaussian MoE. Separation in finite mixture models. In finite-mixture models, quantitative identifiability inequalities connect density estimation to recovery of the mixing measure in Wasserstein distance [ 35 , 17 , 15 ] . For Gaussian location mixtures, Wu and Yang [ 41 ] obtain rates that adapt to separated clusters using moment comparison and polynomial interpolation. Nguyen et al. [ 33 ] further track separation and minimum-weight dependence in single-cluster, multiple-cluster, and unstructured configurations. Extending this perspective to MoE requires an additional step. The mixture atoms now vary with the covariate, and pointwise recovery need not yield a common matching of whole expert functions. Sparse routing also requires control of the probability and geometry of the regions on which particular experts are active. 1.2 Contributions and main findings Our main contribution is to quantify how separation between expert functions affects their recovery from the aggregate conditional density. The likelihood density error has rate log ⁡ n / n \sqrt{\log n/n} for fixed architecture, without a separation assumption. Recovering the individual experts requires an additional inverse step, whose stability depends on their separation. We make this dependence explicit in upper bounds for the experts’ mean absolute errors, showing how the separation penalty changes with cluster structure and the number of simultaneously active experts. Throughout, the Gaussian variance is known and common, and the fitted and true expert counts agree. The rates below hold under the corresponding likelihood, geometry, and restriction hypotheses, with the remaining constants uniform as Δ sep \Delta_{\mathrm{sep}} varies. (i) Separation controls recovery of globally matched dense experts. For dense MoE without a prescribed cluster partition, we obtain the expert recovery bound 𝒪 P ​ ( Δ sep − ( 2 ​ k − 2 ) ​ log ⁡ n / n ) \mathcal{O}_{P}\!\left(\Delta_{\mathrm{sep}}^{-(2k-2)}\sqrt{\log n/n}\right) for the maximum mean absolute error of the matched expert functions over the full covariate domain. One global permutation matches all fitted and true experts. The bound makes explicit how the guarantee deteriorates as the minimum separation decreases, even though the density estimation rate remains unchanged. It requires neither fitted localization nor an error condition relative to separation (Theorem 3.11 and Corollary 5.3 (ii)). Cluster structure refines this dependence. When the true experts form separated clusters with largest size s max s_{\max} , the corresponding bound becomes 𝒪 P ​ ( Δ sep − ( 2 ​ s max − 2 ) ​ log ⁡ n / n ) \mathcal{O}_{P}\!\left(\Delta_{\mathrm{sep}}^{-(2s_{\max}-2)}\sqrt{\log n/n}\right) under one cluster-preserving matching (Theorem 3.6 and Corollary 5.3 (i)). Thus the largest cluster, rather than the total number of experts, governs the displayed penalty for shrinking within-cluster separation, with the between-cluster scale held fixed. Several-cluster recovery requires stable fitted cluster membership and the stated restriction conditions. These results distinguish configurations with the same minimum separation but different cluster sizes. (ii) Sparse routing reduces the separation exponent on active regions. For Top- K K routing with K ≥ 2 K\geq 2 , we obtain the retained-region expert recovery bound 𝒪 P ​ ( C K , λ − 1 ​ Δ sep − ( 2 ​ K − 2 ) ​ log ⁡ n / n ) , \mathcal{O}_{P}\!\left(C_{K,\lambda}^{-1}\Delta_{\mathrm{sep}}^{-(2K-2)}\sqrt{\log n/n}\right), where λ \lambda is a probability threshold and C K , λ C_{K,\lambda} depends on the conditional geometry and restriction constants. The error sums matched expert discrepancies over retained routing regions under the original covariate distribution. Under single-cluster geometry for the active true experts on those regions, the separation exponent is 2 ​ K − 2 2K-2 , compared with 2 ​ k − 2 2k-2 for the dense one-cluster bound (Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 5.6 ). This identifies a way sparse routing can moderate the effect of small separation: fewer Gaussian components need to be distinguished at each input. The regional guarantees also account for exposure. Extending the loss to all routing regions adds a remainder controlled by the square root of their omitted probability; Proposition 5.7 balances this remainder against deterioration of the conditional inverse constant. Matchings may differ across regions, and the target concerns expert values where they are active. Consequently, the smaller separation exponent alone does not establish better full-domain recovery of every latent expert. (iii) Top-1 permits recovery of the selected function without separation. With one active expert, the conditional law is a single Gaussian, and the selected expert function has mean absolute error 𝒪 P ​ ( log ⁡ n / n ) \mathcal{O}_{P}\!\left(\sqrt{\log n/n}\right) without expert-separation or quantitative restriction assumptions (Corollary 4.7 and Eq. ( 5.28 )). This guarantee remains valid when latent experts approach one another or coincide. It identifies the endpoint of the separation dependence: distinguishing simultaneously active components is unnecessary for the selected-function target. Recovering every latent expert under one global matching remains a different objective and requires additional exposure and matching conditions. The deterministic inverse inequalities establish these separation penalties directly for functional recovery losses; the likelihood results transfer them to statistical upper bounds. Verification for linear experts gives concrete settings in which the required assumptions hold. The bounds quantify the effect of separation on the recovery guarantees; matching lower bounds and optimality of the exponents remain open.
